animation.title: The basket detective
animation.analogy: Imagine checking lunch baskets to find snacks that often travel together.

frames.label: 1 · Look
frames.scene: Mark every basket that contains both snacks.
frames.takeaway: Support is a count of baskets, not a feeling about popularity.

frames.label: 2 · Prune
frames.scene: If a smaller snack pair is already rare, cross out every larger basket pattern that contains it.
frames.takeaway: Downward closure saves work before the big search.

frames.label: 3 · Ask
frames.scene: Now ask whether the second snack appears more often after the first snack.
frames.takeaway: Confidence is conditional; lift compares with the background rate.

Represent the cluster by dispersed existing points, not by the mean alone.

animation.title: The toy-box organizer
animation.analogy: Put similar toys together, then check whether the boxes still tell the truth when the toy room grows huge.

frames.scene: Give each toy to the closest box or join boxes using a chosen linkage rule.
frames.takeaway: The distance and geometry decide what “similar” means.

frames.label: 2 · Move the label
frames.scene: For K-means, move each box label to the mean position of its toys and repeat.
frames.takeaway: Each update improves the local squared-error objective, but initialization can still matter.

frames.label: 3 · Tiny summary
frames.scene: Keep confident toys in DS, uncertain groups in CS, and lonely outliers in RS; CURE keeps several boundary representatives.
frames.takeaway: BFR and CURE trade exact detail for a compact, auditable summary.

frames.scene: Count how many toys land in the right labelled box, but also ask whether the boxes are useful and not just tiny.

exercises.label: User-based CF
exercises.prompt: Solve Assignment 2 Question 1(a): center known ratings, compare overlapping entries, then estimate the blanks.
exercises.takeaway: Missing entries stay missing during cosine similarity; normalize the neighbours, average their deviations, and add the target user's mean.
steps: Rows are Alice, Bob, Cathy; columns are Matrix, Inception, Star Wars.
Compute each row mean from known ratings only; a blank is not a zero.
Use only common rated movies for each pair. The centered vectors are shown on their overlaps.
For example, Alice-Bob uses Inception and Star Wars; Alice-Cathy has only Star Wars in common.
Both Bob and Cathy rated Matrix, so average their centered deviations before adding Alice's mean.
Both Alice and Bob rated Inception; use their centered deviations, not raw ratings alone.
$\hat r_{u i}=\bar r_u+\frac{1}{|N_i|}\sum_{v\in N_i}(r_{v i}-\bar r_v)$
This is the normalized-neighbour prediction path; do not turn it into a latent-factor dot product.

exercises.label: Latent factors
exercises.prompt: Solve Assignment 2 Question 1(b): complete Q and Pᵀ from zero reconstruction error on known ratings.
exercises.takeaway: Use the known-rating equations to fill factor entries, then predict the blanks with the completed dot products.
steps: Rows of Q are Alice, Bob, Cathy; columns of Pᵀ are Matrix, Inception, Star Wars.
Use the known Alice-Star Wars rating to solve the missing Alice factor.
Use the known Bob-Matrix rating to solve the missing Bob factor.
The known Alice-Inception rating determines the missing Inception coordinate.
Every known rating now has zero reconstruction error under the given factorization.
The latent-factor estimates are separate from the user-based values in the first tab.

exercises.label: Model boundary
exercises.prompt: Explain the two prediction paths before claiming that their missing ratings should match.
exercises.takeaway: User-based filtering borrows normalized evidence from neighbours; latent factors reconstruct ratings from learned vectors.
steps: $\hat r_{u i}=\bar r_u+\operatorname{avg}_{v\in N_i}(r_{v i}-\bar r_v)$
The evidence is a selected set of similar users and their deviations on item i.
The evidence is a compatible user vector and item vector learned from known ratings.
A neighbourhood deviation is not a latent coordinate and cannot be copied into Q or Pᵀ.
With no rated neighbours, the centred neighbourhood path is undefined; state a prior or cold-start fallback.

splits.label: Boundary case

animation.title: The movie-buddy club

frames.label: 1 · Center

frames.label: 2 · Borrow
frames.scene: Let nearby taste-buddies vote on the missing movie rating.
frames.takeaway: User-based filtering is a neighborhood calculation.

frames.label: 3 · Learn

frames.takeaway: Latent factors predict with a dot product, a different model path.

animation.title: The bouncing web ball
animation.analogy: A ball visits web pages, shares its weight along links, and sometimes jumps to a chosen page.

exercises.prompt: Solve Assignment 2 Question 3 by locating the largest legal bucket and the oldest partial bucket.
exercises.takeaway: For $N=500$, the largest legal bucket is $256$, the worst boundary error is $128$, and an all-one window can have a largest bucket of $128$.
steps: Every bucket has a power-of-two size and there are at most two buckets of each size.
A bucket of size 512 would contain more 1s than the 500-bit window can contain, so 256 is the largest possible size.

DGIM counts half of the oldest partial bucket, so the maximum absolute error is half its size.

exercises.prompt: Solve Assignment 2 Question 4 by separating distinct count, FM's hash signal, and the second frequency moment.
exercises.takeaway: F0 counts distinct values, FM estimates that cardinality, and F2 squares frequencies; these are three different targets.
steps: Value i appears i times, so the stream has 55 total occurrences.
The zeroth moment counts distinct values, not all 55 positions.

exercises.prompt: Work the two AMS cases in Assignment 2 Question 4(d): one sampled position, then all positions averaged.
exercises.takeaway: The one-position estimate is noisy; averaging one variable per position recovers the exact second moment for this stream.
steps: For a sampled position t, f_t is the number of later-or-equal occurrences of the sampled value.
The first position contains value 1, which occurs only once in the whole stream.
This is the answer when the only variable is anchored at the first position.
Average the position estimates after constructing one variable for each stream position.
For a value with frequency i, the terms are 1,3,...,2i-1 and sum to i².

animation.title: The tiny notebook
animation.analogy: A stream is a never-ending parade, so the notebook keeps only a clever summary instead of every visitor.

frames.label: 1 · Recent window
frames.scene: DGIM groups recent 1s into timestamped buckets and keeps at most two buckets of each size.
frames.takeaway: The oldest partly covered bucket explains the count error.

frames.label: 2 · New names

steps: Both advertisers are eligible and have equal remaining budget before the first query.
A tie resolution that gives x to A uses one of A's two y opportunities.
The third and fourth y queries cannot be served because only A bids on y.
Giving the tied x to B preserves A's full budget for two y queries.

exercises.takeaway: Compare remaining budgets only among eligible advertisers, then update exactly the chosen advertiser.

animation.title: The two toy shops
animation.analogy: Two shops have limited coins; each new toy request must be sent to an eligible shop.

dsa5101-dimensionality-reduction.title: Lecture 4 · SVD and CUR reconstruction lab
dsa5101-dimensionality-reduction.learningGoal: Follow the lecture's path from matrix factor shapes to rank selection, power iteration, and interpretable CUR samples.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture 4 supplies the official factorization, error, and CUR workflow; the lab turns each slide-level decision into a worked checkpoint.

exercises.label: SVD shapes
exercises.prompt: Write the full SVD shapes before reasoning about a latent coordinate or a rank-k reconstruction.
exercises.takeaway: Dimensions and orthogonality are the first invariant checks; a shape mismatch invalidates the later projection.
steps: Start with the rectangular matrix and keep the dimensions visible on every factor.
The singular-vector bases preserve inner products even though the diagonal factor changes scale.
The first k left singular directions map an input vector into k latent coordinates.
Use the same retained directions to map the latent coordinates back into the original space.
The projection cannot have rank larger than the number of retained directions.

exercises.label: Rank and energy
exercises.prompt: Use the singular-value spectrum to choose a compact rank and compute both retained energy and squared reconstruction error.
exercises.takeaway: Retained energy is the head of the spectrum; Frobenius error is the squared tail after the rank cutoff.
steps: The singular values are already ordered, so a rank-2 approximation keeps the first two.
The squared Frobenius norm is the sum of all squared singular values.
A rank-2 representation keeps the head energy and discards only the final direction.
Compare the retained energy with the total before claiming that the compression is faithful.
For the squared Frobenius error, sum the squared singular values strictly after the rank boundary.

exercises.label: Power iteration
exercises.prompt: Trace one power-iteration loop and state what converges before using the result as a singular direction.
exercises.takeaway: Each loop applies the operator, normalizes the vector, and checks direction change; scaling is not the target.
steps: Any non-zero starting vector with a component in the dominant direction can begin the iteration.
The matrix amplifies the component associated with the largest magnitude eigenvalue.
Normalization prevents the vector norm from growing without bound while preserving its direction.
Use a direction-change tolerance, not a fixed number of iterations alone, as the convergence check.
At convergence, the vector approximates the dominant eigenvector; apply the connection to $A^TA$ for a right singular vector.

exercises.label: CUR choice
exercises.prompt: Choose sampled columns and rows when the output must remain tied to observed matrix entries, then compare that choice with SVD.
exercises.takeaway: CUR preserves actual rows and columns; SVD gives dense latent directions, so the objective decides the representation.
steps: Importance sampling gives larger probability to columns carrying more squared mass.
Select actual columns J and rows I, with replacement allowed by the sampling procedure.
The pseudoinverse bridge links the sampled row and column spaces to the original matrix.
The reconstruction uses the selected original rows and columns rather than learned dense singular directions.
State the representation requirement before comparing approximation error or storage cost.

animation.title: The shrinking matrix

frames.label: 1 · Factor

frames.takeaway: SVD makes hidden directions explicit.

frames.label: 2 · Compress
frames.scene: Keep the strong singular values and measure the discarded tail.
frames.takeaway: Rank is a trade-off between size and reconstruction error.

frames.label: 3 · Sample
frames.scene: Pick real rows and columns when the summary must stay interpretable.
frames.takeaway: CUR and SVD answer different representation needs.
